newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Fresh data paints cloudy outlook for Germany.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Fresh data paints cloudy outlook for Germany.

text.p: German economic data released on Thursday showed a surge in unemployment during December to a post-war high as well as weaker-than-expected 1996 economic growth that widened the country's budget deficit.

The Federal Labour Office said German unemployment rose 48,000 to a seasonally-adjusted 4.156 million in December, a new post-war record that topped the prior level of 4.1 million in November. The rise was in line with economist expectations.
The unemployment rate, which is based on unadjusted data, rose to 10.8 percent from 10.3 percent in November, the Nuremberg-based office said.

"The figures were a bit disappointing," said economist Gertrud Traud at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt. "We think the negative trend will continue and unemployment will continue to rise until February when it could peak at 11.3 percent."

On an unadjusted basis, some 4.148 million were unemployed, which was below the peak of 4.27 million in February 1996. But Federal Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda said he could not rule out the unadjusted figure soon reaching 4.5 million.

Despite the weak unemployment outlook, several economists did not expect the Bundesbank to reduce interest rates from their already historically-low levels. But others said the German central bank must act to stimulate the economy.
"The Bundesbank cannot just stand by and do nothing when unemployment reaches 4.5 million in two months," said Armin Kayser, economist at SBC Warburg in Frankfurt.
The Bundesbank council meets in Frankfurt on Thursday but no policy decisions are expected.

The German economy also grew provisionally at a real 1.4 percent in 1996, marginally slower than economists' predictions for annual growth for at least 1.5 percent, the German statistics office in Wiesbaden said.
The office said Germany's 1996 budget deficit, critical for membership of the European single currency, was 3.9 percent of GDP compared with 3.5 percent of GDP in 1995.
The Maastricht Treaty, the blueprint for the new currency, sets as a requirement for membership that a country's budget deficit may not exceed three percent of GDP.

The jobless data was also critical for Bonn's currency union goals because it has based financial plans on the assumption that unemployment would average under four million in 1997 - the year whose data will be used to select members.

The German economy was expected to remain weak although conditions were favourable in 1997, the statistics office said. It also noted economic growth during 1996 was mainly driven by exports and capital as well as state spending.

But the office said 1996 growth was only moderate given the conditions and that they assumed there was zero growth on a seasonally-adjusted basis in the 1996 fourth quarter, a time when growth was also slower than 1995 on a year-on-year basis.

Economists have said the present cold weather gripping Germany could hamper construction so much that the economy might contract in the first quarter of 1997 -- as it did a year ago -- with little improvement likely before the spring.

German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said the 1.4 percent growth last year was in line with Bonn's projection of a 1.5 percent expansion and noted conditions were positive for a further improvement and stronger growth in 1997.

"The world economic environment is developing positively, and the conditions for investment have improved," he said. Government budget consolidation will continue and employment will increase, he said.

German financial markets showed little reaction to the data, with 10-year Bund futures modestly paring some losses and the 30-share DAX index showing a muted response while trending lower due to overnight Wall Street losses.
